title: The Merry Wives of Windsor
author: William Shakespeare
setting: Windsor in Shakespeare's own day: the Garter Inn, the Fords' and the Pages' houses, the fields at Frogmore, and Herne's oak in Windsor Park at midnight
lengthNote: About 3,000 lines in five acts, most of them prose; Shakespeare's only comedy set in the England of his own time
openingLine: Sir Hugh, persuade me not. I will make a Star Chamber matter of it.
summary: Falstaff, short of money at the Garter Inn in Windsor, sends the same love letter to two married women, Mistress Ford and Mistress Page, hoping to get at their husbands' money. The wives compare letters and decide to punish him. Three times they draw him on: he is carried out in a basket of dirty laundry and tipped into the Thames, beaten out of the house dressed as an old woman, and finally lured to Herne's oak in Windsor Park at midnight wearing antlers, where children dressed as fairies pinch and burn him. Ford, whose jealousy the wives also cure, has meanwhile disguised himself as 'Master Brook' and paid Falstaff to seduce his own wife. Beside this runs the contest for the Pages' daughter Anne: her father wants Slender, her mother wants Doctor Caius, and Anne marries Fenton.

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of the Complete Works of William Shakespeare (eBook 100)
sourceText.note: Every quotation here is taken word for word from this text, and act, scene and line references follow the traditional Globe numbering, from which modern editions vary by a line or two. This text calls Ford's disguise Brook; the 1602 quarto calls him Broome.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Many editors connect it with the Garter feast of April 1597; others date it a few years later.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: A short quarto; the fuller text is the First Folio's of 1623.

atAGlance.label: Setting
atAGlance.note: Shakespeare's only comedy set in contemporary England, among citizens rather than courtiers.

atAGlance.label: Prose
atAGlance.note: Verse is kept for the lovers and the fairy masque at Herne's oak.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: Two letters
structure.summary: Justice Shallow arrives in Windsor to complain that Falstaff has beaten his men, killed his deer and broken open his lodge, and Sir Hugh Evans, the Welsh parson, proposes to settle it by marrying Shallow's cousin Slender to Anne Page, who has seven hundred pounds. At the Garter Inn Falstaff turns Bardolph into a tapster and reveals his plan to make love to Mistress Ford and Mistress Page, who he says control their husbands' purses. Pistol and Nym refuse to carry his letters and resolve to tell the husbands. At Doctor Caius's house Mistress Quickly, his housekeeper, promises to help Slender, Caius and Fenton to Anne, and Caius challenges Evans for helping Slender.

scenes.title: Shallow's complaint
scenes.summary: Coats of arms, a proposed marriage, a picked pocket, and Slender tongue-tied in front of Anne.

scenes.title: The Garter Inn
scenes.summary: Falstaff cuts his costs, describes the wives as his East and West Indies, and dismisses the two followers who will betray him.

scenes.title: Doctor Caius's house
scenes.summary: Simple hides in a closet, Caius writes a challenge to Evans, and Quickly takes money from Fenton too.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Wives and husbands
structure.summary: Mistress Page and Mistress Ford discover that their letters are identical except for the names, and plan to lead Falstaff on until he pawns his horses. Pistol tells Ford, and Nym tells Page. Page laughs; Ford asks the Host to introduce him to Falstaff as Master Brook. Mistress Quickly brings Falstaff an appointment with Mistress Ford between ten and eleven. Brook then pays him to seduce Mistress Ford, and Falstaff tells him cheerfully about the appointment. Alone, Ford rages. The Host keeps Caius and Evans apart by sending them to different places.

scenes.title: The letters compared
scenes.summary: Letter for letter, but that the name of Page and Ford differs, and two husbands react in opposite ways.

scenes.title: Brook
scenes.summary: Pistol finds the world his oyster, Quickly delivers her message, and Ford in disguise hires the man he suspects.

scenes.title: The duel that does not happen
scenes.summary: Caius waits in a field for Evans while the Host arranges to bring him the wrong way.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: The buck-basket
structure.summary: Evans and Caius meet at last, are disarmed by the Host, and make friends in order to be revenged on him. Ford invites the town to see a monster. Falstaff arrives at Mistress Ford's, Mistress Page runs in with the news that Ford is coming with half Windsor, and they hide Falstaff in a basket of dirty linen that the servants carry out and tip into the Thames at Datchet Mead. Ford searches the house and finds nothing. Anne tells Fenton she will not marry Slender, and would rather be buried alive and bowled to death with turnips than marry Caius. Falstaff, soaked, accepts a second appointment and tells Brook everything.

scenes.title: Frogmore
scenes.summary: The parson sings to keep up his courage, and the Host calls him and the doctor soul-curer and body-curer.

scenes.title: Mistress Ford's house
scenes.summary: Falstaff's courtship, the alarm, the basket and Ford's fruitless search.

scenes.title: Anne and her suitors
scenes.summary: Fenton admits her father's money was his first motive, and Slender courts her through his uncle.

scenes.title: The Thames
scenes.summary: Falstaff describes his alacrity in sinking, and Brook learns about the basket.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: The witch of Brentford
structure.summary: Evans examines young William Page in his Latin while Mistress Quickly hears rude words in every case. At the Fords' house Falstaff is trapped again. Ford checks the basket, so the wives dress Falstaff in the clothes of the fat woman of Brentford, whom Ford calls a witch, and Ford beats him out of the house. The wives then tell their husbands everything, Ford begs his wife's pardon, and the four plan a last public shaming at Herne's oak. Page secretly arranges for Slender to carry off Anne, Mistress Page for Caius to do so, and Anne tells Fenton, who arranges with the Host for a vicar. Three Germans run off with the Host's horses.

scenes.title: William's Latin
scenes.summary: A parson, a schoolboy and a housekeeper who mishears the grammar.

scenes.title: Mother Prat
scenes.summary: The chimney, the kiln-hole, the fat woman's gown, and Ford's cudgel.

scenes.title: Herne the hunter
scenes.summary: The story of the ghost at the oak, and the plan for children dressed as fairies.

scenes.title: Cozened
scenes.summary: The Host loses his horses, and Fenton explains how Anne will deceive both her parents.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Herne's oak
structure.summary: At midnight Falstaff waits at Herne's oak with a buck's head on, calling on Jove, who became a bull and a swan for love. The wives come, then run at a noise of horns, and the fairies, led by Mistress Quickly as their queen, Evans as a satyr and Pistol as Hobgoblin, test him with tapers, find him corrupt, and pinch him. In the confusion Caius and Slender each carry off a boy in disguise, and Fenton carries off Anne. The husbands and wives reveal themselves and mock Falstaff, who admits he has been made an ass. Slender arrives married to a postmaster's boy and Caius to another boy; Fenton and Anne arrive married. Page accepts it, and everyone, Falstaff included, goes home to laugh by a country fire.

scenes.title: Before midnight
scenes.summary: Falstaff promises Brook wonders, and each parent tells a suitor what colour Anne will wear.

scenes.title: The fairies
scenes.summary: The buck's head, the fairy queen's blessing on Windsor Castle, the tapers, and the song of the pinching.

scenes.title: Unmasking
scenes.summary: How like you Windsor wives? The husbands' list of insults, two wrong brides, and Fenton's defence of his marriage.

characters.name: Sir John Falstaff
characters.role: A knight staying at the Garter Inn
characters.summary: Short of money, he decides to court two wives at once for their husbands' purses and sends them the same letter. He is carried out in dirty laundry, thrown in the Thames, beaten as an old woman and pinched by children dressed as fairies, and every time he talks his way back to the next appointment. In the end he admits he has been made an ass and is invited home to supper by one of the husbands.
characters.clue: He tells a stranger called Brook that he will cuckold Ford, not knowing he is talking to Ford.

characters.name: Mistress Ford (Alice)
characters.summary: She receives Falstaff's letter first, carries out the plots in her own house, and has to put up with her husband's searches while she does it. Her jokes about Falstaff are the play's sharpest, and she keeps the plan inside the limits of her honesty.
characters.clue: She says she would be knighted if she would go to hell for an eternal moment or so.

characters.name: Mistress Page (Meg)
characters.summary: The leader of the plotting, and the author of its motto that wives may be merry and yet honest too. She runs in with false alarms, invents the disguise of the fat woman, and proposes the Herne's oak masque. She also plans to marry her daughter to Doctor Caius behind her husband's back, and is beaten by her daughter at her own game.
characters.clue: She suspects the knight has a thousand of these letters, written with a blank space for the name.

characters.name: Master Ford
characters.role: A citizen of Windsor, jealous of his wife
characters.summary: Told by Pistol that Falstaff loves his wife, he disguises himself as Master Brook and pays Falstaff to seduce her, so as to catch her. He searches his house twice, finds nothing, beats an old woman who is Falstaff, and is made a laughing stock until his wife tells him the truth. He asks her pardon and joins the last plot.
characters.clue: He thanks God for his jealousy, and searches a basket of dirty washing twice.

characters.name: Master Page
characters.role: A citizen of Windsor, Anne's father
characters.summary: Confident in his wife, he laughs at Nym's warning and at Ford's searches. He wants his daughter to marry Slender, who has land, and turns Fenton away as too well born and too wild. He ends the play accepting the marriage he tried to prevent.
characters.clue: He says he would turn his wife loose to the knight and let whatever he gets lie on his head.

characters.name: Anne Page
characters.role: The Pages' daughter, with seven hundred pounds
characters.summary: She says little, and every word counts. She sees exactly what three hundred pounds a year does for Slender's faults, would rather be buried alive than marry Caius, and deceives both parents to marry Fenton, the man she has chosen.
characters.clue: She agrees to wear white for her father's man and green for her mother's, and goes off with a third.

characters.name: Fenton
characters.summary: Page objects that he is too high born, that he has spent his money, and that he kept company with the wild Prince and Poins. He admits her father's wealth was his first motive for wooing Anne, and says he found her worth more than money. He arranges their secret marriage through the Host.
characters.clue: He tells Anne her father's wealth was the first motive, and that he now aims at the riches of herself.

characters.name: Abraham Slender
characters.role: Shallow's cousin, Page's choice for Anne
characters.summary: A timid, foolish young man who wishes he had his book of songs and sonnets to woo with, tells Anne about the bear Sackerson, and says he will marry her if his uncle tells him to, hoping that love will decrease upon better acquaintance. He carries off a boy in white and marries him at Eton.
characters.clue: He keeps but three men and a boy, till his mother be dead, and says love may decrease on better acquaintance.

characters.name: Doctor Caius
characters.role: A French physician, Mistress Page's choice for Anne
characters.summary: Hot-tempered and loud, he challenges the parson to a duel for helping Slender, waits for him in the wrong field, and then joins him in revenge on the Host. He carries off a boy in green and marries him at the deanery.
characters.clue: He finds a stranger in his closet and calls for his rapier, and ends the play married to a boy.

characters.name: Sir Hugh Evans
characters.summary: He tries to make peace between Shallow and Falstaff by a marriage, sings to steady his nerves before a duel, examines young William in Latin, teaches the children their fairy parts and plays a satyr at Herne's oak. His Welsh English is mocked by everyone, and he gets the last word on Falstaff's sins.
characters.clue: He says he despises a liar as he despises one that is false, or one that is not true.

characters.name: Mistress Quickly
characters.summary: She keeps the doctor's house single-handed and promises all three of Anne's suitors her help, taking Fenton's money as she does so. She carries the wives' messages to Falstaff and plays the Queen of the Fairies at the oak. She mishears William's Latin as a string of rude words.
characters.clue: She tells three different suitors she knows Anne's mind, and means it every time.

characters.name: The Host of the Garter
characters.summary: Loud and full of nicknames, bully rook and bully Hector among them, he takes on Bardolph as a tapster, arranges the duel and then sends the duellists to the wrong places, helps Ford become Brook and Fenton marry Anne, and loses three horses to men who say they are Germans.
characters.clue: He calls a parson and a doctor soul-curer and body-curer, and is cozened of his horses.

characters.name: Justice Shallow
characters.summary: The same old justice as in Henry IV Part 2, here come to Windsor to complain of Falstaff and to marry his cousin to money. He says he has lived fourscore years and upward.
characters.clue: He threatens to make a Star Chamber matter of a poached deer.

characters.name: Pistol
characters.summary: He refuses to carry the love letter, tells Ford that Falstaff loves his wife, and later plays Hobgoblin in the fairy masque.
characters.clue: He says the world is his oyster, which he with sword will open.

themes.name: Marriage
themes.summary: Two established marriages are tested by Falstaff and by jealousy, and a new one is fought over. The play compares a husband who trusts too easily, a husband who cannot trust at all, and parents who treat a daughter's marriage as a deal.
themes.development: The Fords are reconciled in 4.4, and the play ends with a marriage made by the couple themselves against both parents' plans.

themes.name: Jealousy
themes.summary: Ford's jealousy is the most dangerous thing in Windsor: he pays a stranger to seduce his wife, searches his house with half the town behind him, and beats an old woman he thinks is a witch.
themes.development: It is cured by being made ridiculous. By the end Ford can joke that he will not mistrust his wife until the parson can woo her in good English.

themes.name: Money and love
themes.summary: Falstaff courts for money, Page chooses Slender for his land, Mistress Page chooses Caius for his friends at court, and even Fenton admits that Anne's fortune was his first motive.
themes.development: Anne's line about three hundred pounds a year and Ford's closing couplet, money buys lands, and wives are sold by fate, frame the question the whole plot asks.

themes.name: Disguise and exposure
themes.summary: Ford becomes Brook, Falstaff becomes a bundle of washing, an old woman and a stag, children become fairies, and two boys are married as Anne.
themes.development: Each disguise exposes the person wearing it: Ford's jealousy, Falstaff's appetite, the parents' schemes.

themes.name: A knight among citizens
themes.summary: Falstaff assumes that citizens' wives will be flattered by a knight, and the citizens of Windsor, who have money and sense, prove him wrong.
themes.development: The last scene turns the court's own ceremony, the Order of the Garter, into a blessing spoken by Mistress Quickly over Windsor Castle.

themes.name: English mangled
themes.summary: Evans speaks Welsh English, Caius French English, Mistress Quickly malapropisms, Pistol stage bombast and Nym the word humour. Half the jokes are about how people speak.
themes.development: Falstaff's lowest moment is being mocked by one that makes fritters of English.

techniques.name: Prose against verse
techniques.definition: The switch between prose and verse as a signal of status, mood or place.
techniques.inThisBook: Almost all of Windsor speaks prose. Verse is reserved for Fenton and Anne, for the planning of the masque and for the fairies at Herne's oak, so that the play's romance and its magic sound different from its business.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience knowing more than a character does.
techniques.inThisBook: Falstaff tells Brook about his appointments with Ford's wife, and describes Ford as a cuckoldly knave, while talking to Ford.

techniques.name: Voices
techniques.definition: A way of speaking that belongs to one character.
techniques.inThisBook: Evans's Welsh, Caius's French, Quickly's malapropisms and Nym's humours make every character recognisable by ear and supply much of the comedy.

techniques.name: Foils
techniques.definition: Characters placed side by side so that each shows up the other.
techniques.inThisBook: Page and Ford receive the same warning and react in opposite ways; Slender and Caius are two bad choices set against Fenton.

techniques.name: Wordplay
techniques.inThisBook: Waist and waste, Ford and ford, deer and dear, and a Latin lesson heard as a list of rude words.

techniques.name: The buck-basket
techniques.definition: A physical object on stage that drives the action.
techniques.inThisBook: The basket of dirty linen carries Falstaff out and becomes Ford's obsession; the antlers at Herne's oak finish the joke by putting the cuckold's horns on the would-be seducer.

quotations.text: Indeed, I am in the waist two yards about, but I am now about no waste; I am about thrift.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Explaining his scheme to Pistol and Nym at the Garter.
quotations.analysis: A pun on waist and waste turns his size into a business plan. The joke announces the play's subject: Falstaff's courtship is about money from the start.

quotations.text: they shall be my East and West Indies, and I will trade to them both.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Describing the two wives he plans to court.
quotations.analysis: He speaks of two women as colonies to be traded with. The comedy is in the confidence; the audience has seen neither wife yet and already suspects he is wrong.

quotations.text: Letter for letter, but that the name of Page and Ford differs!
quotations.speaker: Mistress Page
quotations.analysis: The discovery that the letters are identical is the moment the wives stop being flattered and start plotting. Mistress Page goes on to imagine a thousand copies with a blank for the name.

quotations.text: Why then, the world’s mine oyster, Which I with sword will open.
quotations.speaker: Pistol
quotations.context: Falstaff has refused to lend him a penny.
quotations.analysis: The line became a proverb for opportunity. Pistol means he will rob his way through the world, which is why Falstaff answers with a list of the scrapes he has got him out of.

quotations.text: Better three hours too soon than a minute too late.
quotations.speaker: Ford
quotations.context: Alone, after Falstaff has told Brook about the appointment with his wife.
quotations.analysis: Ford's soliloquy is a run of rage, and this proverb is its practical conclusion. His jealousy makes him organised, which is what makes it dangerous.

quotations.text: Buck? I would I could wash myself of the buck! Buck, buck, buck! Ay, buck!
quotations.speaker: Ford
quotations.context: His wife tells him the basket is going to the wash; Falstaff is inside it.
quotations.analysis: Buck-washing was laundering, and a buck was a horned animal. Ford hears the cuckold's horns in a word about laundry while the man he is looking for is carried past him.

quotations.text: O, what a world of vile ill-favoured faults Looks handsome in three hundred pounds a year!
quotations.speaker: Anne Page
quotations.context: Aside, as Slender is brought to woo her.
quotations.analysis: The one rhymed couplet Anne speaks is a price list. She sees exactly why her father favours Slender, and says it only to the audience.

quotations.text: Yet, wooing thee, I found thee of more value Than stamps in gold or sums in sealed bags.
quotations.speaker: Fenton
quotations.context: To Anne, after admitting her father's wealth was his first motive.
quotations.analysis: He begins with an honest admission and ends with a compliment built from the language of money. The play lets its romantic lead confess that he started as a fortune-hunter.

quotations.text: Alas, I had rather be set quick i’ th’ earth, And bowled to death with turnips.
quotations.speaker: Anne Page
quotations.context: Told that her mother favours Doctor Caius.
quotations.analysis: Set quick means buried alive. The comic image of being bowled at with turnips shows how firmly she refuses, without ever raising her voice to her parents.

quotations.text: you may know by my size that I have a kind of alacrity in sinking
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Back at the Garter after being tipped into the Thames.
quotations.analysis: He makes his own humiliation funny before anyone else can. Alacrity usually belongs to quick movement; he attaches it to going under.

quotations.text: Think of that, a man of my kidney, think of that—that am as subject to heat as butter
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Telling Brook, who is Ford, about the basket.
quotations.analysis: The repeated think of that invites pity from the one man who least feels it. The audience enjoys the story twice, once in the telling and once in Ford's face.

quotations.text: Wives may be merry and yet honest too.
quotations.speaker: Mistress Page
quotations.analysis: The line that gives the play its title is a defence of the wives' conduct: they can joke and plot and remain faithful. Honest here means chaste.

quotations.text: As jealous as Ford, that searched a hollow walnut for his wife’s leman.
quotations.speaker: Ford
quotations.context: Asking his neighbours to search his house once more.
quotations.analysis: Ford invents the proverb that will be told against him if he is wrong. He knows he looks ridiculous, and cannot stop.

quotations.text: There is an old tale goes that Herne the hunter, Sometime a keeper here in Windsor Forest,
quotations.speaker: Mistress Page
quotations.context: Proposing the final trick to the husbands.
quotations.analysis: The play turns to local legend and to verse at once. The story of a horned ghost gives the wives a way to put the cuckold's horns on Falstaff himself.

quotations.text: Now, good Sir John, how like you Windsor wives?
quotations.speaker: Mistress Page
quotations.context: After the fairies have pinched him and the husbands have come forward.
quotations.analysis: The question names the play's heroines and settles the contest: the town has beaten the knight.

quotations.text: I do begin to perceive that I am made an ass.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Faced with the husbands and wives at Herne's oak.
quotations.analysis: He has just pulled off the buck's head, and the horns are being held up for the husbands to see. His admission is slow and dignified, and the play lets him keep his wit even at the bottom.

quotations.text: Have I lived to stand at the taunt of one that makes fritters of English?
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Evans has told him that cheese is not good to give putter.
quotations.analysis: Falstaff can bear being tricked by the wives; being corrected by the Welsh parson is the last straw. His pride is in his language.

quotations.text: In love, the heavens themselves do guide the state. Money buys lands, and wives are sold by fate.
quotations.speaker: Ford
quotations.context: After Fenton explains his marriage to Anne.
quotations.analysis: Ford, who began the play buying a chance to test his wife, ends it with a couplet separating love from money. The rhyme gives the plot its moral in the voice of its most reformed character.

timeline.label: Lord Hunsdon elected to the Order of the Garter
timeline.detail: The Lord Chamberlain, patron of Shakespeare's company, was elected in April; many editors connect the Garter speech in 5.5 with the feast.

timeline.label: Henry IV Part 1 printed
timeline.detail: Falstaff was already a famous stage character; the first part of Henry IV was printed this year and reprinted the next.

timeline.label: First quarto printed
timeline.detail: A short text in which Ford's disguise is called Broome.

timeline.label: Played at court
timeline.detail: The Revels Accounts record a performance before King James on 4 November.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The full text, printed as the third of the comedies.

timeline.label: John Dennis's story of the Queen's command
timeline.detail: Dennis wrote that the play was written at Elizabeth's command in fourteen days; Nicholas Rowe added in 1709 that she wanted to see Falstaff in love.

timeline.label: Nicolai's Die lustigen Weiber von Windsor
timeline.detail: Otto Nicolai's comic opera, first performed in Berlin.

timeline.label: Verdi's Falstaff
timeline.detail: Verdi's last opera, with a libretto by Boito drawn mainly from this play, first performed at La Scala.

timeline.label: Vaughan Williams's Sir John in Love
timeline.detail: An opera setting the play with English folk songs.

places.name: Windsor
places.note: The town, the Garter Inn and the Fords' and Pages' houses.

places.name: Windsor Home Park
places.note: Herne's oak, where the last scene is set.

places.name: Datchet Mead
places.note: Where the buck-basket is tipped into the Thames.

places.name: Frogmore
places.note: The field where the parson waits for the doctor.

places.name: Eton
places.note: Where Slender marries a postmaster's boy.

places.name: Brentford
places.note: Home of the fat woman whose gown Falstaff wears.

criticalViews.summary: Set among merchants' households rather than courts, the play gives its victory to the townspeople and particularly to the wives, who defend their reputations with wit and a laundry basket.
criticalViews.counter: The last scene ends with a blessing on Windsor Castle and the Order of the Garter, so the play also flatters the court it seems to leave behind.

criticalViews.summary: Many critics have felt that this Falstaff, gulled three times, is a lesser figure than the Falstaff of Henry IV, who is never outwitted for long.
criticalViews.counter: Verdi and many modern productions have made the play's Falstaff a great comic role in his own right, and his wit survives every humiliation.

criticalViews.summary: Mistress Ford and Mistress Page plan and carry out every trick, cure a husband's jealousy and keep their honesty. They are among the most capable women in Shakespeare's comedies.
criticalViews.counter: Their power has limits: Mistress Page's own plan for her daughter fails, and the play's last marriage is arranged by the young couple and the Host.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare present the wives of Windsor?
plan: Start with the comparison of the letters in 2.1 and the decision to be revenged.
Examine the three tricks and who plans each one.
Consider 'Wives may be merry and yet honest too' as the play's defence of them.
Weigh Mistress Page's failed plan for Anne.
Conclude on how far the play gives the wives control.

essayQuestions.question: How is jealousy dramatised through Ford?
plan: Contrast Ford's and Page's reactions to the same warning.
Analyse the Brook scenes and Ford's soliloquies.
Look at the two searches and the beating of the old woman.
Conclude on whether the play treats jealousy as a comic or a serious fault.

essayQuestions.question: What part does money play in love and marriage in the play?
plan: Begin with Falstaff's plan to court the wives' purses.
Compare the three suitors and why each parent chooses one.
Analyse Anne's couplet on three hundred pounds a year and Fenton's admission.
Conclude on the play's final view of money and love.

discussionQuestions: Does Falstaff deserve all three punishments?
Why does Ford disguise himself as Brook instead of simply watching his wife?
Is Page a good husband and a bad father?
Anne hardly speaks. How does the play still make her the winner?
Why do so many characters in this play speak English badly?
Is the ending, with Falstaff invited to supper, a fair one?

related.why: Falstaff at his best, with Hal at the Boar's Head.
Falstaff, Shallow, Pistol and Mistress Quickly before Windsor.
Another comedy of disguise and a gulled would-be lover.
Another comedy in which a jealous man is fooled and a marriage is at stake.
